When the Weed Wars Came to Warren Street
New York has embarked on a radical experiment: legalizing marijuana as an act of reparations to heal the wounds of America’s drug war. I went upstate to Hudson to see if it could be done.

This trendy river town, once a drug-war epicenter, is now one of America’s most unequal cities. It seemed like a perfect testing ground for a law designed to repair the drug war’s “racially disparate impact.”
Hudson’s “green rush” would draw an incredible cast of characters, including the boxer Mike Tyson and the heiress Abby Rockefeller — whose uncle was an architect of the drug war.
I followed the saga of two competitors vying to corner the local weed market: Bill Hughes, a Black Hudson native, and Joanne Wilson, a white entrepreneur from Manhattan.
The story I found in Hudson was full of surprising turns. It showed, in real time, what can happen when the ideals of racial justice meet the realities of capitalism.
Howard Gibson, Kenny Holston/The New York Times
